## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89519.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89519.4.sa1)

Plasticity in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) is thought to underlie the formation of associative memories between neutral and aversive stimuli, i.e. fear memory. Concomitantly, fear learning modifies the expression of BLA theta rhythms, which may be supported by local interneurons. Several of these interneuron subtypes, PV+, SOM+, and VIP+, have been implicated in the acquisition of fear memory. However, it was unclear how they might act synergistically to produce BLA rhythms that structure the spiking of principal neurons so as to promote plasticity. Cattani et al. explored this question using small network models of biophysically detailed interneurons and principal neurons.

Using this approach, the authors had four principal findings:

(1) Intrinsic conductances in VIP+ interneurons generate a slow theta rhythm that periodically inhibits PV+ and SOM+ interneurons, while disinhibiting principal neurons.

(2) A gamma rhythm arising from the interaction between PV+ and principal neurons establishes the precise timing needed for spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

(3) Removal of any of the interneuron subtypes abolishes conditioning-related plasticity.

(4) Learning-related changes in principal cell connectivity enhance expression of slow theta in the local field potential.

The strength of this work is that it explores the role of multiple interneuron subtypes in the formation of associative plasticity in the basolateral amygdala. The authors use biophysically detailed cell models that capture many of their core electrophysiological features, which helps translate their results into concrete hypotheses that can be tested in vivo. Moreover, they try to align the connectivity and afferent drive of their model with those found experimentally.

A drawback to this study is the construction of the afferent drive to the network, which does not elicit activities that are consistent with the majority of those observed to similar stimuli. The authors discuss this issue in depth, and provide potential mechanisms that may overcome it.

Setting aside the issues with the conditioning protocol, the study offers a model for the generation of multiple rhythms in the BLA that is ripe for experimental testing. The most promising avenue would be in vivo experiments testing the role of local VIP+ neurons in the generation of slow theta. That would go a long way to resolving whether BLA theta is locally generated or inherited from medial prefrontal cortex or ventral hippocampus afferents.

The broader importance of this work is that it illustrates that we must examine the function of neurons not just in terms of their behavioral correlates, but by their effects on the microcircuit they are embedded within. No one cell type is instrumental in producing fear learning in the BLA. Each contributes to the orchestration of network activity to produce plasticity. Moreover, this study reinforces a growing literature highlighting the crucial role of theta and gamma rhythms in BLA function.

results.result: The model demonstrates that three classes of BLA interneurons (VIP, SOM, and PV) generate distinct rhythms based on their biophysical properties: VIP cells with D-current produce low theta (~3.5 Hz) with nested gamma bursts (~38 Hz), SOM cells with NaP- and H-currents produce high theta (~12 Hz), and PV cells interact with excitatory neurons to produce PING gamma rhythms.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C12-C15, and C56-C59 collectively demonstrate through model simulations (Figures 1A-C) that each interneuron type produces specific rhythms matching their biophysical properties. The model reproduces experimental electrophysiological behaviors and generates rhythms consistent with experimental observations, providing strong computational evidence for the mechanistic origins of BLA rhythms.

results.result: All three interneuron types (VIP, SOM, PV) are necessary for spike-timing-dependent plasticity between CS-encoding (ECS) and fear-encoding (F) neurons during fear learning. Removal of any single interneuron type prevents learning, with only full networks showing robust potentiation of the ECS-to-F synapse within 40 seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C30, C32-C33, C41-C43, and C61 demonstrate through systematic ablation studies (Figures 3A-B, 5D) that all network realizations with complete interneuron populations become learners, while networks lacking any interneuron type fail to show plasticity. The mechanistic explanations in C35, C38-C39 provide computational evidence for how each cell type contributes to the necessary timing and pauses for depression-dominated STDP.

results.result: PV interneurons establish the correct pre-post spike timing between ECS and F neurons through PING (pyramidal-interneuron network gamma) rhythms, with differential lateral versus feedback inhibition biasing ECS to fire before F.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 and C70-C71 describe a specific mechanistic role for PV cells supported by model simulations (Figure 4A). The model demonstrates that reciprocal PV-F connections create PING rhythms that establish fine temporal ordering necessary for potentiation, with weaker lateral inhibition to ECS than feedback inhibition to F creating the required pre-post timing.

results.result: The depression-dominated STDP rule requires periodic pauses in excitatory neuron activity to prevent accumulated depression. VIP and SOM interneurons create these pauses through rhythmic inhibition, allowing depression to decay and enabling potentiation during active phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C62, C72-C74 provide a mechanistic explanation supported by model simulations (Figure 4, Appendix 1-figure 2C) showing that continuous PING activity leads to depression unless interrupted. The model demonstrates that VIP pauses allow SOM activation, which inhibits ECS and F, creating the necessary breaks for the depression-dominated rule to produce net potentiation.

results.result: Fear conditioning produces a selective increase in low theta power (2.5-4 Hz) but not high theta power in both network spiking activity and LFP. This low theta increase occurs only in learning networks and is absent in non-learners, establishing it as a biomarker of successful fear conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47, C54-C55, C65-C66 are strongly supported by model simulations (Figure 6A-E) showing statistically significant low theta increases in learners but not non-learners. The results replicate experimental findings from Davis et al. 2017 and extend them by demonstrating the biomarker property through comparison of learner versus non-learner networks, providing novel computational predictions.

results.result: The low theta power increase after fear conditioning is mechanistically driven by AMPA currents to PV interneurons, which show a dramatic 3000-fold power increase relative to baseline, compared to only 4.6-fold for GABA currents. This results from the newly potentiated ECS-to-F pathway activating F, which then drives PV cells at low theta frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 provide a detailed mechanistic explanation supported by quantitative model analysis (Figure 6F-G). The specific power ratios (3×10³ for AMPA vs 4.6 for GABA across 20 realizations) provide strong quantitative evidence. The causal chain from learned pathway to F activation to PV excitation is clearly demonstrated in the model simulations.

results.result: A heterogeneous network with multiple neurons of each type (3 interneurons per subtype, 10 excitatory neurons per type) robustly produces fear learning, with all full network realizations becoming learners in less than 40 seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 demonstrate model robustness through expansion from single-cell to multi-cell networks (Figure 5). The results show that the core findings generalize beyond the minimal model to more realistic heterogeneous networks, strengthening confidence in the model's predictions.

results.result: The necessity of all interneuron types for learning depends specifically on the depression-dominated plasticity rule. With classical Hebbian plasticity (lower depression than potentiation amplitude), learning could occur without VIP and SOM cells, but the depression-dominated rule provides regulatory control over plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77, C106-C108 are supported by comparative model simulations (Appendix 1-figure 4) showing that alternative plasticity rules change interneuron requirements. This demonstrates that the model's core finding about interneuron necessity is conditional on the specific plasticity rule used, which is appropriately acknowledged and mechanistically explained.

results.result: During fear conditioning, US activates both F and VIP neurons, with VIP disinhibiting F by inhibiting SOM and PV. Before US onset, VIP shows low theta bursting, SOM fires at high theta, PV is silent, and F is inhibited. After US onset, F becomes active during VIP active phases, PV provides feedback inhibition, and ECS fires before F creating appropriate timing for potentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C29 describe the detailed network dynamics during fear conditioning supported by model simulations (Figure 2A-C). The temporal sequence of activation patterns and the resulting conductance changes are clearly demonstrated, showing how the circuit configuration and rhythms interact to produce the conditions for plasticity.

results.result: The depression-dominated plasticity rule may prevent overgeneralization of fear learning. VIP cells may establish this rule through co-release of VIP peptide with GABA, which can inhibit potentiation via second messenger pathways involving VPAC1 receptors present in the amygdala.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 present a speculative hypothesis about the functional role of the depression-dominated rule and a potential molecular mechanism involving VIP peptide. While the cited evidence (C80-C83) supports the existence of relevant molecular machinery, the causal connection to the plasticity rule and overgeneralization prevention remains hypothetical and untested in the model.

results.result: Neuromodulators (acetylcholine from basal forebrain and dopamine) released during US presentation may provide sustained depolarization and increased excitability of ECS and F neurons lasting 7-10 seconds to 20 minutes, potentially resolving the temporal overlap problem when CS and US stimuli do not overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C117, C119 present a hypothesis about how neuromodulators could enable STDP when CS and US don't temporally overlap. While individual citations support neuromodulator release and effects (C109-C114, C116), the integrated hypothesis about sustained activity enabling plasticity (C115, C117) is speculative and not directly tested in the model, which assumes overlap by design.

results.result: Experimental evidence suggests BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations. The model demonstrates that interneuron intrinsic currents (D-current in VIP, NaP- and H-currents in SOM) can affect LFP and support theta/gamma rhythm generation, consistent with slice studies showing intrinsic theta generation with ACh stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 connect experimental findings about intrinsic BLA theta generation to the model's mechanisms. The model results (Figure 6G) demonstrate that interneuron intrinsic currents contribute to LFP rhythms, providing a mechanistic explanation for experimental observations. The implicit modeling of ACh effects through VIP activation (C97) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: The model predicts that blocking D-current in VIP interneurons or silencing any interneuron subtype will prevent fear learning. The model assumes weak ECS-to-PV connections to preserve PING rhythm integrity necessary for proper ECS-F timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 present testable predictions and model assumptions. The predictions (C102, C105) follow logically from the model's demonstrated necessity of each interneuron type. The assumption about ECS-to-PV connectivity (C103-C104) is justified mechanistically and represents a clear hypothesis that could be tested experimentally.

results.result: Fear learning involves distributed networks including medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus beyond the amygdala. These structures may provide substrates for sustained BLA neuron firing after US offset and are crucial for fear extinction, which involves high theta rhythms and acquisition of distinct safety memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 summarize established knowledge from experimental literature about distributed fear networks and extinction mechanisms. These claims appropriately contextualize the model's focus on BLA circuits within the broader neuroscience of fear learning, though they are not directly tested in the current model.

results.result: Low theta rhythms observed in BLA may originate from multiple sources: intrinsic BLA generation, respiratory-related oscillations from olfactory bulb via prefrontal cortex, or volume conduction. High theta may originate from hippocampus during spatial exploration and memory processes involved in fear conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 acknowledge alternative sources for rhythms observed in BLA LFP recordings, appropriately citing experimental evidence. This represents important caveats about rhythm origins that don't undermine the model's demonstration that BLA interneurons can generate these rhythms intrinsically.

results.result: The BLA is the main site of fear learning through synaptic plasticity, showing prominent low theta, high theta, and gamma rhythms in LFP recordings. Experimental studies show increased low theta and gamma after fear conditioning, while high theta modulation is associated with fear extinction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C8-C11 establish the experimental and theoretical background for the study through citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge about BLA's role in fear learning and the rhythms observed experimentally, providing appropriate context for the modeling work.

results.result: The model may apply broadly to associative learning situations beyond fear conditioning because it uses interneuron types (PV, SOM, VIP) commonly found throughout cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 presents a speculative generalization about the model's applicability. While the ubiquity of these interneuron types in cortex is established knowledge, whether the specific mechanisms demonstrated for fear learning generalize to other forms of associative learning remains untested and speculative.

results.result: Experimental fear conditioning typically achieves learning after one or few CS-US pairings (1.5-2 s) with 30-40 s intervals. The model defines learners as networks with ECS-to-F conductance >0.12 mS/cm³ at 40 s, resulting in systematic F activation following ECS spikes during CS-only presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C34 establish the experimental context and model definition of learning. C31 accurately cites experimental timescales, while C34 provides a clear operational definition of learning in the model that connects synaptic strength to functional output, appropriately justified by the resulting behavior.

results.result: PV interneurons and excitatory projection neurons form PING (pyramidal-interneuron network gamma) rhythms when reciprocally connected and the excitatory neuron receives sufficient input. PING frequency depends on external input to the excitatory neuron and PV's inhibitory decay time constant (8.3 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 describe the PING mechanism demonstrated in the model (Figure 1C) and cite established literature (Whittington et al., 2000). The model successfully reproduces this well-characterized rhythm-generating mechanism and identifies the key parameters controlling its frequency.

results.result: BLA SOM cells are not necessarily the only source of high theta observed during fear learning; high theta in BLA LFP also originates from prefrontal cortex and/or hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 appropriately acknowledge limitations in attributing high theta solely to BLA SOM cells, citing experimental evidence for external sources. This represents appropriate scientific caution about interpreting the model's results in light of known anatomical connectivity.

results.result: STDP requires overlap in pre- and post-synaptic firing. The depression-dominated rule used in the model makes depression stronger than potentiation unless there is fine timing in gamma and low theta cycles, with each interneuron contributing to establishing this timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 describe fundamental properties of STDP and the specific plasticity rule used in the model. C67 states general STDP principles, while C68-C69 characterize the depression-dominated rule's requirements, which are demonstrated through model simulations and mechanistic analysis.

results.result: The model demonstrates that VIP, PV, and SOM interneurons in the BLA are critically involved in producing experimentally observed rhythms through their intrinsic biophysical properties: VIP cells generate low theta via D-current, PV cells produce gamma through PING interactions with excitatory cells, and SOM cells contribute to high theta via NaP- and H-currents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'Intrinsic conductances in VIP+ interneurons generate a slow theta rhythm' and noting the model 'explores how biophysical properties of different interneuron subtypes in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) enable production of oscillations.' The use of 'biophysically detailed cell models that capture many of their core electrophysiological features' is praised as a strength.

results.result: The rhythms produced by interneurons, particularly the gamma rhythm arising from PV-principal neuron interactions, promote the formation of a dedicated fear circuit by establishing precise spike timing needed for spike-timing-dependent plasticity between CS-encoding and fear-encoding neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a principal finding, stating 'A gamma rhythm arising from the interaction between PV+ and principal neurons establishes the precise timing needed for spike-timing-dependent plasticity.' They note the work 'highlights the importance of interactions between interneurons for some forms of spike-timing dependent plasticity.'

results.result: Each class of interneurons (VIP, PV, SOM) is necessary for plasticity during fear learning. Removal of any interneuron type abolishes conditioning-related plasticity, with only the full network containing all three interneuron types showing robust potentiation and successful learning within experimentally relevant timeframes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this as a principal finding: 'Removal of any of the interneuron subtypes abolishes conditioning-related plasticity.' They note this demonstrates that 'No one cell type is instrumental in producing fear learning in the BLA. Each contributes to the orchestration of network activity to produce plasticity.'

results.result: Fear conditioning leads to an increase in low theta power (but not high theta) in both network spiking activity and LFP, consistent with experimental findings. This low theta increase occurs only in learners and not in non-learners, establishing it as a biomarker of successful fear conditioning.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a principal finding: 'Learning-related changes in principal cell connectivity enhance expression of slow theta in the local field potential.' They note the model 'replicates the experimental increase in the low theta after successful training' and acknowledge consistency with experimental data.

results.result: The depression-dominated plasticity rule requires periodic pauses in excitatory cell activity (provided by VIP and SOM cells) and fine timing in gamma cycles (provided by PV cells) to enable potentiation. Without pauses, continuous firing leads to depression rather than potentiation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this mechanistic explanation as part of the model's framework. They note the work uses 'biophysically detailed cell models' and explores 'mechanisms of plasticity thought to underlie associative learning' without raising concerns about this specific mechanism. The depression-dominated rule is treated as a valid modeling choice.

results.result: The model reproduces experimentally observed electrophysiological properties of BLA interneurons: VIP cells show gamma bursts nested in low theta rhythm, SOM cells fire at high theta frequencies (~12 Hz), and PV cells are silent at baseline but form PING rhythms with excitatory neurons when activated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the model's biophysical realism, noting it uses 'biophysically detailed cell models that capture many of their core electrophysiological features, which helps translate their results into concrete hypotheses that can be tested in vivo.' No concerns are raised about these baseline properties.

results.result: The low theta power increase after fear conditioning is mechanistically driven by AMPA currents to PV interneurons, which are activated by the newly potentiated pathway from CS-encoding to fear-encoding neurons. AMPA currents show a dramatic power increase (3×10³ fold) compared to GABA currents (4.6 fold).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this mechanistic explanation as part of the model's findings without raising concerns. The mechanistic detail is consistent with their recognition that the model provides 'concrete hypotheses that can be tested in vivo' and explores network mechanisms underlying plasticity.

results.result: The model addresses the temporal mismatch between CS and US in some fear conditioning paradigms by proposing that neuromodulators (acetylcholine from basal forebrain and dopamine) induce sustained depolarization and increased excitability in BLA neurons, enabling overlap of CS and US-driven activity necessary for STDP.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this as a limitation: 'A drawback to this study is the construction of the afferent drive to the network, which does not elicit activities that are consistent with the majority of those observed to similar stimuli.' However, they acknowledge 'The authors discuss this issue in depth, and provide potential mechanisms that may overcome it,' suggesting the neuromodulator hypothesis is plausible but not fully validated.

results.result: The model predicts that blockade of D-current in VIP interneurons or silencing of any interneuron subtype will both diminish low theta and prevent fear learning, providing testable experimental predictions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this prediction, stating 'The most promising avenue would be in vivo experiments testing the role of local VIP+ neurons in the generation of slow theta. That would go a long way to resolving whether BLA theta is locally generated or inherited from medial prefrontal cortex or ventral hippocampus afferents.' They view these predictions as experimentally testable and valuable.

results.result: The depression-dominated plasticity rule (as opposed to classical Hebbian plasticity) allows for regulation by all interneuron types and may prevent pathological overgeneralization of fear learning, though learning could theoretically occur without VIP and SOM cells under a classical Hebbian rule.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this theoretical discussion as part of the model's framework. They note the work explores 'some forms of spike-timing dependent plasticity' without challenging the choice of plasticity rule or the theoretical reasoning about its functional advantages.

results.result: The model's proposal that BLA can intrinsically generate theta oscillations is consistent with recent experimental evidence showing theta generation in BLA slices with inhibition removed or ACh stimulation, with interneurons' intrinsic currents contributing to LFP rhythms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers view this as a key contribution, stating the study 'offers a model for the generation of multiple rhythms in the BLA that is ripe for experimental testing' and that testing VIP neuron involvement 'would go a long way to resolving whether BLA theta is locally generated or inherited from medial prefrontal cortex or ventral hippocampus afferents.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support claims about interneuron types producing specific rhythms (C3, C56-C59). OpenEval provides more comprehensive coverage including C12-C15 about model validation, while peer review focuses specifically on VIP+ interneurons generating slow theta and praises the biophysical detail.

Both evaluations support the role of PV+ interneurons in generating gamma rhythms for STDP timing (C35, C70-C71). OpenEval focuses on mechanistic details of PING rhythms and temporal ordering, while peer review explicitly recognizes this as a principal finding about gamma rhythm establishing precise timing for plasticity.

Both evaluations strongly support the necessity of all interneuron types for plasticity (C5, C30, C32-C33, C41-C43, C61). OpenEval emphasizes systematic ablation studies and mechanistic explanations, while peer review explicitly identifies this as a principal finding that 'no one cell type is instrumental' and each contributes to orchestration.

Both evaluations support claims about low theta increases as a learning biomarker (C6, C44-C47, C54-C55, C65-C66). OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance and replication of experimental findings, while peer review explicitly recognizes this as a principal finding about learning-related connectivity changes enhancing slow theta expression.

Both evaluations support the mechanistic role of VIP pauses enabling SOM activation for depression-dominated STDP (C38-C39, C62, C68-C69, C72-C74). OpenEval provides detailed mechanistic explanation with figure references, while peer review implicitly accepts this as part of the biophysically detailed framework without raising concerns.

Both evaluations support the mechanistic explanation of how learned pathways enhance low theta through AMPA vs GABA power ratios (C48-C53). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence and causal chains, while peer review accepts this as providing concrete testable hypotheses.

Both evaluations support the model's biophysical realism and network dynamics during fear conditioning. OpenEval covers detailed temporal sequences (C18-C29), while peer review affirms the biophysically detailed cell models capture core electrophysiological features (C12-C17, C20-C25).

Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN the neuromodulator hypothesis for enabling STDP without temporal overlap (C109-C117, C119). OpenEval notes the hypothesis is speculative and untested in the model, while peer review identifies this as a limitation regarding afferent drive construction but acknowledges the authors discuss potential mechanisms.

Both evaluations support claims about intrinsic BLA theta generation and interneuron contributions to rhythms (C9, C91-C98). OpenEval emphasizes mechanistic explanations from model results, while peer review views this as a key contribution offering a testable model for multiple rhythm generation in BLA.

Both evaluations support the testable predictions about interneuron necessity and VIP neuron involvement (C102, C105). OpenEval notes predictions follow logically from demonstrated necessity, while peer review explicitly endorses testing VIP+ neurons as 'the most promising avenue' for resolving rhythm generation questions.

Both evaluations support claims about alternative plasticity rules changing interneuron requirements (C75-C77). OpenEval emphasizes this demonstrates conditionality appropriately acknowledged, while peer review implicitly accepts the theoretical discussion about plasticity rule choices (also covering C78 about functional advantages).

OpenEval supports model robustness through expansion to multi-cell networks (C40-C42), demonstrating generalization beyond minimal models. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific robustness claims.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the speculative hypothesis about depression-dominated rule preventing overgeneralization and VIP peptide mechanisms (C78-C84). Peer review R10 only addresses C75-C78 about plasticity rules, not the overgeneralization prevention hypothesis.
OpenEval supports claims contextualizing the model within broader fear networks and extinction mechanisms (C85-C90). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextualization claims.

OpenEval supports acknowledgment of alternative rhythm sources in BLA (C99-C101). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer review does discuss rhythm origin questions in other contexts.
OpenEval supports background claims about BLA's role in fear learning and observed rhythms (C1-C2, C8-C11). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background establishment claims.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the speculative generalization about model applicability to other associative learning forms (C7). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this generalization claim.
OpenEval supports claims establishing experimental context and operational definition of learning (C31, C34). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these definitional claims.

OpenEval supports claims about PING mechanism reproduction (C16-C17). While peer review R6 covers overlapping claims about biophysical properties, it doesn't specifically evaluate the PING mechanism claims.

OpenEval supports appropriate acknowledgment of limitations in attributing high theta to BLA SOM cells (C63-C64). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific limitation acknowledgments.

OpenEval supports claims about STDP fundamentals and depression-dominated rule requirements (C67-C69). While peer review R5 covers C68-C69 as part of VIP mechanism evaluation, it doesn't separately evaluate these foundational STDP claims.
